41988.m: In Guatemala's civil war it was mainly the Maya who suffered.

41989.q: Which organisation set up the truth commission for El Salvador?
41989.e: The commission set up by the UN investigated crimes in the civil war from 1980 to 1992. Its 1993 report is called “From Madness to Hope”.
41989.m: The UN investigated the crimes in El Salvador's civil war.

41990.q: Which country did Mobutu Sese Seko rule as a dictator?
41990.e: Mobutu ruled the Congo from 1965 to 1997. From 1971 to 1997 the country was called Zaire.
41990.m: Mobutu Sese Seko ruled the Congo, which he called Zaire.

41991.q: How did Mobutu come to power in 1965?
41991.e: Mobutu was head of the army and seized power in a coup in 1965. After that he allowed no more real elections.
41991.m: Mobutu seized power in a military coup in 1965.

41992.q: Which new name did Mobutu give his country in 1971?
41992.e: Mobutu renamed the country Zaire in 1971, after an old name for the Congo river. Since 1997 it has been called the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
41992.m: Under Mobutu the Congo was called Zaire from 1971 to 1997.

41993.q: Which item of clothing was Mobutu's trademark?
41993.e: Mobutu almost always appeared with a leopard-skin hat and a walking stick. The hat was meant to show strength and African tradition.
41993.m: Mobutu's trademark was a leopard-skin hat.

41994.q: Which famous boxing match took place in Mobutu's capital Kinshasa in 1974?
41994.e: In 1974 Muhammad Ali beat George Foreman in Kinshasa. Mobutu used the fight to make his country known around the world.
41994.m: The “Rumble in the Jungle” took place in Kinshasa in 1974.

41995.q: What did Mobutu do with his country's wealth?
a: He shared it out among the poor
He gave it to the UN
41995.e: Mobutu moved a huge fortune abroad while the people stayed poor. Rule like this is called kleptocracy, “rule by thieves”.

41996.q: How did Mobutu lose power in 1997?
41996.e: Rebels under Laurent-Désiré Kabila captured Kinshasa in 1997. Mobutu fled into exile and died the same year.
41996.m: Mobutu was driven out by rebels in 1997.

41997.q: Why did Western countries such as the USA support Mobutu for a long time?
a: He was seen as an ally against communism
41997.e: During the Cold War the USA and other Western countries saw Mobutu as a partner against the Soviet Union. That is why they overlooked his oppression for a long time.
41997.m: During the Cold War the West backed Mobutu as an opponent of communism.

41998.q: Which country did Robert Mugabe rule?
41998.e: Mugabe was prime minister from 1980 and President of Zimbabwe from 1987 to 2017.

41999.q: Which European country ruled present-day Zimbabwe as a colony?
41999.e: Zimbabwe was a British colony and was called Rhodesia at that time. It became independent in 1980.
41999.m: Zimbabwe was a British colony called Rhodesia.

42000.q: What did Zimbabwe achieve in 1980 after a long war of liberation?
a: Victory at a football World Cup
42000.e: After a long war of liberation Zimbabwe became independent in 1980. Mugabe won the first elections and became head of government.

42001.q: Which economic problem reached its peak in Zimbabwe in 2008?
42001.e: Money lost its value so quickly that there were banknotes of 100 trillion Zimbabwe dollars. In 2009 the country's own currency was abandoned.
42001.m: In Zimbabwe money became almost worthless in 2008.

42002.q: What did Mugabe's government often seize by force from 2000?
42002.e: In the so-called land reform many farms of white large landowners were occupied. After that farming collapsed badly.
42002.m: Mugabe's land reform led to a collapse in farming.

42003.q: How did Mugabe's rule end in 2017?
a: The army forced him to resign
He handed the office to his son
42003.e: In November 2017 the military took control. Mugabe then resigned at the age of 93.
42003.m: Mugabe had to resign in 2017 under pressure from the army.

42004.q: Who became President of Zimbabwe after Mugabe resigned in 2017?
42004.e: Emmerson Mnangagwa had long been Mugabe's vice president. After Mugabe resigned he took over the presidency.
42004.m: Mugabe's vice president became his successor in 2017.

42005.q: What did observers often accuse Robert Mugabe of at elections?
a: Too many candidates on the list
School opening hours that were too short
42005.e: At elections in Zimbabwe opposition figures were threatened and results were doubted. In this way Mugabe's party ZANU-PF stayed in power.
42005.m: Mugabe also held on to power through unfair elections.

42006.q: How long was Robert Mugabe in power altogether?
42006.e: Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe from 1980 to 2017, first as prime minister and then as president.
42006.m: Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years.

42007.q: What does the Afrikaans word “apartheid” mean?
42007.e: In Afrikaans apartheid means roughly “apartness”. It referred to the legal separation of people by skin colour.
42007.m: Apartheid means separation by skin colour.

42008.q: In which country was there a system of apartheid?
42008.e: Apartheid was the state system of racial segregation in South Africa. A white minority ruled over the black majority.

42009.q: Who held power in South Africa during apartheid?
42009.e: Only white people were allowed to vote for parliament. In this way a small white minority ruled over the black majority.
42009.m: During apartheid a white minority ruled.

42010.q: What were black South Africans not allowed to do during apartheid?
42010.e: Black people had no vote for parliament. They also had to use separate schools, buses and residential areas.
42010.m: During apartheid black people were not allowed to vote.

42011.q: How were schools, buses and residential areas organised during apartheid?
42011.e: White and black people had to use separate schools, buses, beaches and residential areas. The facilities for black people were usually much worse.
42011.m: Apartheid separated people by skin colour.

42012.q: How did many countries around the world react to apartheid?
a: With boycotts and sanctions against South Africa
They praised South Africa for it
42012.e: Many countries stopped buying goods from South Africa. For a long time South Africa was also not allowed to take part in the Olympic Games.
42012.m: The world put pressure on South Africa with boycotts.

42013.q: About how long was Nelson Mandela in prison?
42013.e: Mandela fought against apartheid and was imprisoned for it. In 1990 he was released after about 27 years.
42013.m: Nelson Mandela was in prison for 27 years.

42014.q: When were the first elections held in South Africa in which all adults were allowed to vote?
42014.e: In April 1994 all adults were allowed to vote for the first time, whatever the colour of their skin. Queues kilometres long formed outside the polling stations.
42014.m: In 1994 South Africa held its first free elections for everyone.

42015.q: Who became South Africa's first black president in 1994?
42015.e: After the first free elections Nelson Mandela became president. He worked for reconciliation.
42015.m: Nelson Mandela became President of South Africa in 1994.

42016.q: Which country did Muammar al-Gaddafi rule?
42016.e: Gaddafi ruled Libya from 1969 to 2011. That means he was in power for more than 40 years.
42016.m: Muammar al-Gaddafi ruled Libya for more than 40 years.

42017.q: How did Gaddafi come to power in 1969?
a: He overthrew the king in a coup
He was put in place by the UN
42017.e: As a young officer Gaddafi overthrew King Idris in 1969. After that he ruled without free elections.
42017.m: Gaddafi overthrew the Libyan king in 1969.

42018.q: What was the book in which Gaddafi wrote down his political ideas called?
42018.e: In “The Green Book” Gaddafi described his own idea of the state. Green was also the colour of the Libyan flag under his rule.
42018.m: Gaddafi's ideas were set out in “The Green Book”.

42019.q: What exploded over the Scottish town of Lockerbie in 1988?
42019.e: 270 people died. A Libyan intelligence officer was convicted for it, and Libya under Gaddafi was held responsible.
42019.m: Libya was held responsible for the Lockerbie bombing of 1988.

42020.q: How did Libya react in 2008 when Geneva police arrested Gaddafi's son?
a: It held two Swiss men in the country
42020.e: Hannibal Gaddafi was arrested for mistreating his staff. Libya then held two Swiss businessmen in the country for a long time.
42020.m: The arrest of Gaddafi's son in Geneva led to the Libya crisis of 2008.

42021.q: What did Gaddafi propose about Switzerland in 2009?
a: To divide it among its neighbours
To admit it to the African Union
To make it the UN headquarters
42021.e: During the crisis with Switzerland Gaddafi called for the country to be divided between Germany, France and Italy. Nobody anywhere took the proposal seriously.
42021.m: In 2009 Gaddafi called for Switzerland to be divided up.

42022.q: As part of which wave of protests did the uprising against Gaddafi happen in 2011?
42022.e: After Tunisia and Egypt, people in Libya also rose up in 2011. This turned into a civil war in which NATO intervened with air strikes.
42022.m: The uprising against Gaddafi was part of the Arab Spring.

42023.q: How did Gaddafi's life end in October 2011?
a: He died in exile in Venezuela
He died in a prison in The Hague
He was voted out by the people
42023.e: Gaddafi was captured in his home town of Sirte. Shortly afterwards he was killed by rebel fighters.
42023.m: Gaddafi was killed by rebels near Sirte in 2011.

42024.q: What is the name of Libya's capital, where Gaddafi had his seat of government?
42024.e: Gaddafi's headquarters was the Bab al-Aziziya fortress in Tripoli. The 2011 uprising, on the other hand, began in Benghazi in the east.

42025.q: Which country did Saddam Hussein rule?
42025.e: Saddam Hussein was President of Iraq from 1979 to 2003. He ruled with violence and a large secret service.
42025.m: Saddam Hussein was dictator of Iraq.

42026.q: How many parties really had a say in Iraq under Saddam Hussein?
42026.e: Saddam Hussein's Baath Party ruled Iraq on its own. Other political groups were persecuted.
42026.m: In Iraq under Saddam Hussein only his Baath Party ruled.

42027.q: Against which neighbouring country did Saddam Hussein wage war from 1980 to 1988?
42027.e: The First Gulf War between Iraq and Iran lasted eight years. Hundreds of thousands of people died without either side winning.
42027.m: The war between Iraq and Iran lasted from 1980 to 1988.

42028.q: Which small neighbouring country did Saddam Hussein have occupied in 1990?
42028.e: In August 1990 the Iraqi army invaded Kuwait. An international coalition led by the USA drove it out again in early 1991.
42028.m: Saddam Hussein had Kuwait occupied in 1990.

42029.q: Which ethnic group in Iraq was attacked with poison gas in Halabja in 1988?
42029.e: About 5,000 people died in the poison gas attack on the Kurdish town of Halabja. It is regarded as one of the regime's worst crimes.
42029.m: In 1988 Saddam Hussein had Kurds in Halabja killed with poison gas.

42030.q: In which year was Saddam Hussein overthrown by an invasion led by the USA?
42030.e: In March 2003 the USA and its allies attacked Iraq. Baghdad fell in April, and Saddam's government collapsed.

42031.q: Where was Saddam Hussein found in December 2003?
a: In a hole in the ground near Tikrit
On a ship in the Persian Gulf
42031.e: US soldiers found him in a camouflaged hole in the ground on a farm near his home town of Tikrit. He had been hiding for months.
42031.m: Saddam Hussein hid in a hole in the ground near Tikrit.

42032.q: What happened to Saddam Hussein in December 2006?
42032.e: A special Iraqi court sentenced him to death for killing 148 people in the town of Dujail. He was hanged on 30 December 2006.

42033.q: Which picture from Baghdad in April 2003 became a worldwide symbol of Saddam's fall?
a: The toppling of his big statue
42033.e: In Firdos Square in Baghdad a large statue of Saddam was pulled down. The pictures went round the world.
42033.m: The toppling of Saddam's statue in Baghdad became the symbol of the end of his rule.

42034.q: Which country did Ferdinand Marcos rule?
42034.e: Marcos was President of the Philippines from 1965 to 1986. From 1972 he ruled as a dictator.

42035.q: What did Marcos impose in September 1972 so that he could rule with almost unlimited power?
42035.e: With martial law Marcos closed parliament and had opponents arrested. It lasted until 1981.
42035.m: From 1972 Marcos ruled under martial law.

42036.q: What did Marcos' wife Imelda become known for around the world?
42036.e: After the family fled, well over a thousand pairs of shoes were found in the presidential palace. They became a symbol of waste.
42036.m: Imelda Marcos became known for her huge shoe collection.

42037.q: What happened to the opposition leader Benigno Aquino when he returned to the Philippines in 1983?
a: He was shot at the airport
He received a medal from Marcos
42037.e: Benigno Aquino was killed just as he got off the plane. His death set off huge protests against Marcos.
42037.m: The murder of Benigno Aquino in 1983 strengthened resistance to Marcos.

42038.q: How was Ferdinand Marcos overthrown in 1986?
a: Through peaceful protests by huge numbers of people
42038.e: Hundreds of thousands of people gathered peacefully on the streets of Manila. Marcos had to leave the country in February 1986. This is called the People Power Revolution.
42038.m: A peaceful popular uprising overthrew Marcos in 1986.

42039.q: What was special about Corazon Aquino, who followed Marcos in 1986?
a: She was the first female President of the Philippines
42039.e: Corazon Aquino was the widow of the murdered Benigno Aquino. She became the first woman to lead the Philippines.
42039.m: In 1986 Corazon Aquino became the first female President of the Philippines.

42040.q: What did the Federal Council do in 1986 with Marcos' money in Swiss banks?
a: It gave it to the Red Cross
42040.e: After Marcos was overthrown, the Federal Council froze his accounts in Switzerland. Later the Philippines got back about 680 million US dollars from them.
42040.m: Switzerland froze Marcos' money in 1986 and later returned it.

42041.q: What did Ferdinand Marcos have to do after he was overthrown in 1986?
a: He had to leave the country
42041.e: With the help of the USA, Marcos fled with his family to Hawaii. He died there in 1989.
42041.m: After he was overthrown Marcos had to go into exile.

42042.e: Suharto was President of Indonesia from 1967 to 1998. He ruled in an authoritarian way for more than 30 years.
42042.m: Suharto ruled Indonesia for more than 30 years.

42043.q: How did Suharto come to power in Indonesia from 1965?
a: With the help of the army
As the son of a king
42043.e: After 1965 General Suharto pushed the first president, Sukarno, out of power step by step.
42043.m: Suharto came to power with the help of the army.

a: In an authoritarian way, with the help of the army
Not at all, he was only king
42044.e: Suharto called his rule the “New Order”. Critics were persecuted, and the army had great power.
42044.m: Suharto ruled Indonesia in an authoritarian way.

42045.q: Against whom were the mass killings in Indonesia in 1965 and 1966, which went along with Suharto's rise, directed?
42045.e: After a failed coup attempt in 1965 the army hunted down communists. Estimates range from 500,000 to one million deaths.
42045.m: During Suharto's rise hundreds of thousands of alleged communists were killed.

42046.q: Suharto had East Timor occupied in 1975. What did East Timor later become?
42046.e: Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975. East Timor became independent in 2002.
42046.m: East Timor has been independent since 2002.

42047.q: What led to Suharto's resignation in 1998?
a: An economic crisis and huge protests
A victory at the football World Cup
42047.e: In the Asian financial crisis the Indonesian currency crashed and prices rose sharply. After huge protests Suharto resigned in May 1998.
42047.m: An economic crisis and protests led to Suharto's resignation in 1998.

42048.q: Why did Suharto have only one name?
a: Many people on Java have only one name
42048.e: On the island of Java it is common to have only one name. His predecessor Sukarno also had only one name.
42048.m: Like many Javanese, Suharto had only one name.

42049.q: What is the name of Indonesia's capital, from which Suharto ruled?
42049.e: Jakarta is on the island of Java. The big protests against Suharto also took place there in 1998.

42050.q: What was Myanmar called before the military government changed the name in 1989?
42050.e: The military government renamed the country Myanmar in 1989. In English the old name Burma is still widely used.
42050.m: Myanmar used to be called Burma.

42051.q: Who has ruled Myanmar for most of the time since 1962?
42051.e: Myanmar's army is called the Tatmadaw. It has ruled the country for most of the time since 1962.
42051.m: In Myanmar the army has ruled most of the time.

42052.q: What happened in Myanmar in February 2021?
a: The military removed the elected government
The first free elections were held
42052.e: On 1 February 2021 the army took power. Elected politicians were arrested.
42052.m: In 2021 the military staged a coup in Myanmar.

42053.q: Who led the coup in Myanmar in 2021?
42053.e: General Min Aung Hlaing was head of the army. After the coup he took over the leadership of the country.
42053.m: The 2021 coup was led by the head of the army.

42054.q: Who led the Saffron Revolution against the military government in Myanmar in 2007?
42054.e: Thousands of monks in saffron-coloured robes marched peacefully through the streets. The military crushed the protests by force.
42054.m: The Saffron Revolution of 2007 was led by monks.

42055.q: What did Myanmar's military government have built from scratch around 2005?
42055.e: The government moved the capital from Yangon to the newly built city of Naypyidaw in the interior of the country.
42055.m: Myanmar has a newly built capital.

42056.q: Which Muslim minority fled from the violence of Myanmar's army to Bangladesh in 2017?
42056.e: After attacks by the army, more than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in 2017. The UN speaks of serious crimes.
42056.m: The Rohingya had to flee Myanmar in 2017.

42057.q: Why is a popular uprising in Myanmar called the “8888 Uprising”?
42057.e: On 8 August 1988 nationwide protests against military rule began. The military cracked down on them brutally.

42058.q: Which country does the politician Aung San Suu Kyi come from?
42058.e: Aung San Suu Kyi is Myanmar's best-known opposition politician. She fought for decades against military rule.
42058.m: Aung San Suu Kyi is a politician from Myanmar.

42059.q: Which prize did Aung San Suu Kyi receive in 1991?
42059.e: She received the Nobel Peace Prize for her non-violent struggle for democracy. As she was under house arrest, her sons accepted the prize.
42059.m: Aung San Suu Kyi received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991.

42060.q: Who was Aung San, the father of Aung San Suu Kyi?
42060.e: General Aung San led Burma to independence. He was murdered in 1947, when his daughter was two years old.
42060.m: Aung San Suu Kyi's father Aung San was a hero of independence.

42061.q: How did Aung San Suu Kyi spend about 15 years between 1989 and 2010?
42061.e: The military government repeatedly locked her up in her house in Yangon. She was released in November 2010.
42061.m: Aung San Suu Kyi was under house arrest for about 15 years.

42062.q: What did Aung San Suu Kyi fight for for decades?
42062.e: Aung San Suu Kyi campaigned without violence for free elections and against military rule.
42062.m: Aung San Suu Kyi fought for democracy.

42063.q: Who seized power in Myanmar in a coup in 2021?
a: The people at the ballot box
42063.e: On 1 February 2021 the army staged a coup and removed the elected government. Since then the military has ruled again.
42063.m: Since 2021 the military has ruled Myanmar again.

42064.q: What was Aung San Suu Kyi strongly criticised for internationally?
a: Her silence about the persecution of a Muslim minority
42064.e: From 2017 the army drove out hundreds of thousands of Rohingya. Aung San Suu Kyi even defended Myanmar before the International Court of Justice.
42064.m: Aung San Suu Kyi was strongly criticised over the Rohingya crisis.

42065.q: What happened to Aung San Suu Kyi after the military coup of 2021?
a: She became head of the army
42065.e: The army arrested her on the day of the coup. After that she was sentenced to many years in prison in several trials.
42065.m: After the 2021 coup Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested.

42066.q: From which country did Eritrea become independent in 1993?
42066.e: After a 30-year war of independence the population voted in 1993 to separate from Ethiopia.
42066.m: Eritrea has been independent from Ethiopia since 1993.

42067.q: What is special about the President of Eritrea (as of 2026)?
a: He has ruled since 1993 without a presidential election
He is elected again every year
He is also King of Ethiopia
He rules the country from Switzerland
42067.e: Isaias Afwerki has been president since independence in 1993. Since then there has been no national presidential election in Eritrea.
42067.m: Eritrea has had the same president since 1993, without a free election.

42068.q: Which sea does Eritrea lie on?
42068.e: Eritrea is on the Horn of Africa. Its long coastline borders the Red Sea.
42068.m: Eritrea lies on the Red Sea.

42069.e: Eritrea is in the east of Africa, on the Red Sea. Its capital is Asmara.
42069.m: Eritrea is a country in Africa.

42070.q: Eritrea used to be a colony. What does that mean?
a: A foreign country ruled over Eritrea
42070.e: A colony is ruled by a foreign country. Eritrea was an Italian colony from 1890 to 1941.
42070.m: Eritrea used to be an Italian colony.

42071.q: What is one main reason why many young people flee from Eritrea?
a: The national service with no time limit
A ban on going to school
A shortage of water across the whole country
42071.e: National service is officially limited to 18 months, but it often lasts many years. It is regarded as forced labour under strict control.
42071.m: Many Eritreans flee from the endless national service.

42072.q: Which statement about press freedom in Eritrea is true?
a: There are a particularly large number of private broadcasters
Journalists are given special protection by the state
The press can freely criticise the government
42072.e: Since 2001 all independent media have been banned, and many journalists are in prison without trial. For years Eritrea has been right at the bottom of the press freedom rankings.
42072.m: There is no free press in Eritrea.

42073.q: What is Eritrea's significance for the Swiss asylum system?
a: Eritreans are among the largest groups of asylum seekers
Eritrea takes in most refugees from Switzerland
Eritrea is the favourite holiday destination of Swiss families
Switzerland has never taken in asylum seekers from Eritrea
42073.e: Since about 2010 people from Eritrea have made a particularly large number of asylum applications in Switzerland. Today tens of thousands of Eritreans live in Switzerland.
42073.m: Many asylum seekers in Switzerland come from Eritrea.

42074.q: Which country does Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo rule (as of 2026)?
42074.e: Obiang has been President of Equatorial Guinea since 1979. The small country is in Central Africa on the Gulf of Guinea.

42075.q: How long has Teodoro Obiang been in power (as of 2026)?
42075.e: Obiang came to power in a coup in August 1979. That makes him one of the longest-ruling heads of state in the world.
42075.m: Teodoro Obiang has been in power since 1979.

42076.e: The previous dictator, Francisco Macías Nguema, was Obiang's uncle. After the coup he was sentenced to death and executed.
42076.m: In 1979 Obiang overthrew his uncle Macías Nguema.

42077.q: Which official language makes Equatorial Guinea unique in Africa?
42077.e: Equatorial Guinea was a Spanish colony. It is the only country in Africa with Spanish as an official language; French and Portuguese are also official languages.
42077.m: Equatorial Guinea is the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa.

42078.q: Which raw material has brought Equatorial Guinea a lot of money since the 1990s?
42078.e: Since oil was discovered, the country has been one of the richest in Africa per person. Even so, a large part of the population lives in poverty.
42078.m: In Equatorial Guinea it is mainly the ruling family that profits from oil.

42079.q: What did the Geneva authorities seize from Obiang's son Teodorín in 2016?
42079.e: The Geneva public prosecutor seized Teodorín's expensive sports cars. In 2019, 25 of his cars were auctioned and raised about 27 million francs.
42079.m: In 2016 Geneva seized Teodorín Obiang's luxury cars.

42080.q: Which office does Obiang's son Teodorín hold in Equatorial Guinea (as of 2026)?
42080.e: Teodorín Nguema Obiang Mangue is the country's vice president. Critics see this as an attempt to keep power in the family.
42080.m: Obiang's son Teodorín is vice president.

42081.q: Which big football tournament did Equatorial Guinea host on its own in 2015?
42081.e: In 2015 Equatorial Guinea stepped in at short notice to host the Africa Cup of Nations. It had already co-hosted the tournament with Gabon in 2012.
42081.m: Equatorial Guinea hosted the Africa Cup of Nations in 2015.

42082.q: On which continent did the dictator Jean-Bédel Bokassa rule?
42082.e: Bokassa ruled the Central African Republic from 1966 to 1979. Before that he was head of the army.
42082.m: Jean-Bédel Bokassa ruled the Central African Republic.

42083.q: What did Bokassa proclaim himself in 1976?
42083.e: Bokassa proclaimed the Central African Empire and called himself Emperor Bokassa I. The country was desperately poor.

42084.q: Which famous ruler did Bokassa imitate at his coronation in 1977?
42084.e: Bokassa admired Napoleon and modelled his coronation on Napoleon's. The lavish ceremony swallowed up a large part of the state budget.
42084.m: Bokassa had himself crowned on the model of Napoleon.

42085.q: What did Bokassa's lavish coronation in 1977 cost his poor country?
a: A large part of the state budget
Only the cost of a village party
42085.e: Bokassa had himself crowned with a crown, a throne and a carriage. The ceremony swallowed up a lot of money, although the people in the country were desperately poor.
42085.m: Bokassa's coronation was expensive while the people were poor.

42086.q: How did Bokassa come to power?
42086.e: On New Year's Eve 1965/66 the army chief Bokassa overthrew his cousin, President David Dacko. After that he ruled as sole ruler.
42086.m: Bokassa came to power through a coup.

42087.q: Which crime of 1979 led to Bokassa's downfall?
a: The killing of schoolchildren after protests
The theft of England's crown jewels
42087.e: Schoolchildren had protested against expensive compulsory school uniforms. Many of them were arrested and killed, and Bokassa was involved.
42087.m: The murder of schoolchildren in 1979 cost Bokassa his power.

42088.q: Which country removed Bokassa from power in 1979 while he was abroad?
42088.e: In “Opération Barracuda” French troops brought the former president David Dacko back to power. Bokassa was in Libya at the time.
42088.m: France removed Bokassa from power in 1979.

42089.q: What happened to Bokassa after he returned voluntarily in 1986?
a: He was put on trial and convicted
He became President of the African Union
He was sent abroad again at once
42089.e: Bokassa was sentenced to death, but the sentence was changed to imprisonment. He was released in 1993 and died in 1996.
42089.m: Bokassa was convicted after his return but not executed.

42090.q: In which country did the Arab Spring begin at the end of 2010?
42090.e: The protests began in Tunisia in December 2010 and then spread to many Arab countries.
42090.m: The Arab Spring began in Tunisia.

42091.q: In which square in Cairo did hundreds of thousands of demonstrators gather in 2011?
42091.e: Tahrir Square in the centre of Cairo became the symbol of the Egyptian revolution of 2011.
42091.m: Tahrir Square in Cairo was the heart of the Egyptian protests.

42092.q: Which Egyptian president resigned in February 2011 after about 30 years in power?
42092.e: Hosni Mubarak had ruled Egypt since 1981 and resigned on 11 February 2011 after weeks of mass protests.
42092.m: Hosni Mubarak had to step down in 2011 after mass protests.

42093.q: What did many people demand in the Arab Spring?
a: More freedom and an end to dictatorship
42093.e: People protested against oppression, corruption and poverty. They wanted to have a say and to live freely.
42093.m: In the Arab Spring people demanded freedom.

42094.q: In which country did the protests of 2011 lead to a long civil war with millions of refugees?
42094.e: In Syria the government of Bashar al-Assad crushed the protests by force, and this turned into a civil war lasting years.
42094.m: In Syria protests turned into a devastating civil war.

42095.q: Which tools did many young demonstrators use to organise protests in the Arab Spring?
42095.e: Calls to protest and pictures spread very quickly via Facebook, Twitter and mobile phone videos, even when governments partly blocked the internet.
42095.m: Social media helped spread protests quickly in the Arab Spring.

42096.q: Who overthrew Egypt's first freely elected president, Mohamed Morsi, in 2013?
42096.e: After mass protests the army under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi removed President Morsi in July 2013.
42096.m: In Egypt the military took power again in 2013.

42097.q: Which country is seen as the only one where the Arab Spring at first led to a democracy?
42097.e: After the revolution Tunisia adopted a democratic constitution and held free elections, while other countries fell into war or a new dictatorship.
42097.m: For a long time Tunisia was seen as the success story of the Arab Spring.

42098.q: Which event of 1968 does the name “Arab Spring” recall?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
42098.e: The Prague Spring of 1968 was an attempt at reform in Czechoslovakia; the word “spring” stands for a new beginning and renewal.
42098.m: In political movements the word “spring” stands for a new beginning.

42099.q: What were people in Tunisia mainly protesting against at the end of 2010?
a: Poverty, unemployment and an authoritarian president
42099.e: Many young people had no work, and criticism of the government was forbidden. When a young vegetable seller was driven to despair by the arbitrary behaviour of the authorities, protests broke out across the country.
42099.m: Poverty and oppression set off the Jasmine Revolution.

42100.q: What is the wave of protests that spread from Tunisia to many Arab countries in 2011 called?
42100.e: After Tunisia there were also big protests in Egypt, Libya, Syria and other countries. This period is called the Arab Spring.
42100.m: The Arab Spring began in Tunisia.

42101.q: What happened to the Tunisian president Ben Ali in January 2011?
42101.e: Ben Ali had ruled Tunisia in an authoritarian way for a long time. On 14 January 2011, after weeks of protests, he left the country.
42101.m: President Ben Ali fled abroad from the people's anger in 2011.

42102.q: What is the revolution in Tunisia in 2010 and 2011 called?
42102.e: The revolution in Tunisia was named after the jasmine. It led to President Ben Ali having to leave the country in 2011.
42102.m: The revolution in Tunisia is called the Jasmine Revolution.

42103.q: Where does the Jasmine Revolution get its name from?
a: The protests began in a jasmine garden
42103.e: Jasmine is widespread in Tunisia and is regarded as the national flower; that is why the revolution was named after it.
42103.m: The Jasmine Revolution is named after Tunisia's national flower.

42104.q: Which prize did a Tunisian group receive in 2015 for its work for democracy?
42104.e: The National Dialogue Quartet, made up of a trade union, employers, a human rights league and lawyers, mediated in a serious crisis in 2013. For this it received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2015.
42104.m: In 2015 a Tunisian group received the Nobel Peace Prize for Tunisia's path to democracy.

42105.q: What did Tunisia give itself in 2014 after the revolution?
42105.e: After the revolution an elected assembly drew up a new constitution. It was adopted in January 2014.
42105.m: Tunisia got a new democratic constitution in 2014.

42106.q: How did Ben Ali rule Tunisia until 2011?
a: In an authoritarian way, critics were persecuted
Together with seven ministers, as in Switzerland
As president for just one year
42106.e: Ben Ali came to power in 1987 and ruled with a firm hand for more than 20 years. Criticising him was dangerous.
42106.m: Ben Ali ruled Tunisia in an authoritarian way for more than two decades.

42108.q: What was Gandhi protesting against with the famous Salt March of 1930?
42108.e: The British banned Indians from producing salt themselves and taxed it; Gandhi marched to the sea and, as a symbol, made salt himself.
42108.m: With the Salt March Gandhi deliberately broke an unjust law.

42109.q: What is a boycott, like the one Gandhi used against British goods?
a: Buying as many goods as possible
42109.e: Gandhi called on people to stop buying British cloth. In this way he wanted to put pressure on the British without violence.
42109.m: A boycott is a peaceful way of applying pressure.

42110.q: In which country did Gandhi work as a lawyer for about 20 years before returning to India?
42110.e: Gandhi lived in South Africa from 1893 to 1914 and there fought for the first time, without violence, against discrimination against Indians.
42110.m: Gandhi first developed his non-violent resistance in South Africa.

42113.q: What did Gandhi demand in 1942 with the call “Quit India”?
a: The British should leave India at once
42113.e: “Quit India” means “Leave India”. The British then arrested Gandhi and many other leaders.
42113.m: With “Quit India” Gandhi demanded an end to British rule in 1942.

42114.q: How did Mahatma Gandhi die in January 1948?
a: He died during a hunger strike
He was killed in an accident
42114.e: A Hindu extremist shot Gandhi in New Delhi on 30 January 1948.
42114.m: Gandhi was murdered by an extremist in 1948.

42115.q: In which city was Václav Havel born in 1936?
42115.e: Havel came from a wealthy Prague family, which is why the Communists later refused him entry to some schools.
42115.m: Václav Havel was born in Prague.

42116.q: What did people in Prague do in November 1989 to make the Communist government resign?
a: They demonstrated peacefully in large numbers
42116.e: Hundreds of thousands took to the streets peacefully. Havel and his fellow campaigners then negotiated the handover of power with the government.
42116.m: Peaceful mass protests brought about change in Prague in 1989.

42117.q: What is the peaceful overthrow of 1989 in Czechoslovakia called?
42117.e: Because the change of power happened almost without violence, people speak of the “Velvet Revolution”.
42117.m: The Velvet Revolution of 1989 was almost completely non-violent.

42118.q: According to Havel's well-known motto, which two values should prevail over lies and hatred?
42118.e: The sentence “Truth and love must prevail over lies and hatred” became the motto of the Velvet Revolution.
42118.m: Havel believed truth and love would win over lies and hatred.

42121.q: Which country was Havel president of from 1993?
42121.e: After the peaceful division of Czechoslovakia in 1993, Havel became the first President of the Czech Republic and remained so until 2003.
42121.m: In 1993 Havel became the first President of the Czech Republic.

42122.q: What did Václav Havel urge people living in a dictatorship to do?
a: Stay honest and not join in the lies
42122.e: In his essay “Living in Truth” Havel described how honest behaviour can weaken a regime's lies.
42122.m: Havel urged people to live in truth, even in a dictatorship.

42123.q: Which system of racial segregation did Nelson Mandela fight against?
42123.e: Apartheid separated people in South Africa by skin colour and put the black majority at a disadvantage.
42123.m: Nelson Mandela fought against apartheid in South Africa.

42125.q: Off which South African city is the prison island of Robben Island?
42125.e: Robben Island lies in Table Bay, a few kilometres off Cape Town.
42125.m: Robben Island lies off the coast of Cape Town.

42126.q: What did the prisoners on Robben Island have to do?
a: Do hard labour in the quarry
42126.e: The prisoners had to dig limestone in the quarry. The glaring light damaged Mandela's eyes.
42126.m: On Robben Island the prisoners had to work in the quarry.

42129.q: With whom did Mandela share the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993?
42129.e: Mandela and de Klerk, the last apartheid president, received the prize together for the peaceful end of apartheid.
42129.m: Mandela and de Klerk were honoured together for ending apartheid.

42130.q: What has Robben Island been since 1999?
a: A nature reserve with no visitors
42130.e: The former prison is now a museum and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as a symbol of victory over oppression.
42130.m: The former prison on Robben Island is now a museum and World Heritage Site.

42131.q: Which country did the civil rights campaigner Liu Xiaobo come from?
42131.e: Liu Xiaobo was a Chinese literary critic and human rights activist.
42131.m: Liu Xiaobo campaigned for human rights in China.

42132.q: Which award did Liu Xiaobo receive in 2010 while he was in prison?
42132.e: He received the Nobel Peace Prize for his non-violent struggle for human rights in China.
42132.m: Liu Xiaobo was given the Nobel Peace Prize while he was in prison.

42133.q: What stood on the stage in Liu Xiaobo's place at the 2010 Nobel Prize ceremony?
42133.e: Neither Liu nor his family were allowed to travel to Oslo; the empty chair became a symbol.
42133.m: The empty chair in Oslo was a reminder of the imprisoned Liu Xiaobo.

42134.q: What did Liu Xiaobo call for in 2008 together with others in a public appeal?
a: Free elections and freedom of speech
More power for the Communist Party
42134.e: The appeal was called Charter 08. Among other things it called for the separation of powers, free elections and freedom of speech.
42134.m: With Charter 08 Chinese citizens called for democratic reforms.

42135.q: Why was Liu Xiaobo sentenced to a long prison term in 2009?
a: Because he called for democracy and freedom
Because he had caused an accident
Because he rode his bike without a light
42135.e: A court in Beijing sentenced him to 11 years in prison for “inciting subversion of state power”. In reality he was punished for his opinions.
42135.m: Liu Xiaobo was sentenced to 11 years in prison for his opinions.

42136.q: At which event in Beijing in 1989 did Liu Xiaobo go on hunger strike?
a: At the protests in Tiananmen Square
At the fall of the Berlin Wall
At an election to the People's Congress
42136.e: Liu supported the student protests and, on the night of the crackdown, helped many students leave the square.
42136.m: Liu Xiaobo supported the student protests in Beijing in 1989.

42137.q: How did Liu Xiaobo's life end in 2017?
a: He died in exile in the USA
He was released and died later
42137.e: Liu Xiaobo died of liver cancer in July 2017 without ever being free again.
42137.m: Liu Xiaobo died a prisoner in 2017.

42138.q: What happened to Liu Xiaobo's wife Liu Xia, even though she was never charged?
a: She was under house arrest for years
42138.e: Liu Xia lived cut off under house arrest for years and was only allowed to leave for Germany in 2018.
42138.m: The families of critics of a regime are often punished too.

42139.q: In which country was Alexei Navalny the best-known opposition politician?
42139.e: For years Navalny was the best-known critic of President Vladimir Putin.
42139.m: Alexei Navalny was Russia's best-known opposition politician.

42140.q: What is Navalny's foundation FBK mainly known for?
42140.e: The Anti-Corruption Foundation published videos and investigations into the wealth of politicians.
42140.m: Navalny exposed corruption in Russia through his investigations.

42141.q: What happened to Alexei Navalny in August 2020?
a: He was poisoned with a nerve agent
42141.e: Navalny became seriously ill on a flight in Siberia. Laboratories found a nerve agent from the Novichok group.
42141.m: In 2020 Navalny only just survived being poisoned.

42142.q: In which city was Navalny treated after his poisoning in 2020?
42142.e: He was flown to the Charité hospital in Berlin and recovered there.
42142.m: After the poisoning Navalny was saved in Berlin.

42143.q: What happened when Navalny returned to Russia in January 2021?
a: He was arrested right at the airport
He founded a government in exile
He was expelled from the country
42143.e: The police arrested him straight after he landed in Moscow; after that he was sentenced to long prison terms.
42143.m: Navalny returned to Russia despite the danger and was arrested.

42144.q: What was the title of Navalny's well-known 2021 investigative video about a huge estate on the Black Sea?
42144.e: The video was watched tens of millions of times within a few days and sparked protests.
42144.m: With the video “A Palace for Putin” Navalny reached an audience of millions.

42145.q: Where did Alexei Navalny die in February 2024?
a: In a prison camp in the Arctic
In a prison in St Petersburg
42145.e: Navalny died on 16 February 2024 in a penal colony north of the Arctic Circle.
42145.m: Navalny died in 2024 as a prisoner in an Arctic prison camp.

42146.q: Who has carried on Navalny's political work since 2024?
42146.e: After her husband's death Yulia Navalnaya announced that she would continue his work from abroad.
42146.m: Yulia Navalnaya is carrying on her husband's work.

42147.q: Which country does the opposition politician Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya come from?
42147.e: Tsikhanouskaya stood against Alexander Lukashenko in the presidential election in Belarus in 2020.
42147.m: Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya is an opposition leader from Belarus.

42148.q: Why did Tsikhanouskaya stand for president in 2020?
a: She was the government's favourite candidate
She was nominated by the military
42148.e: Her husband, the blogger Siarhei Tsikhanouski, wanted to stand and was arrested; she stood in his place.
42148.m: Tsikhanouskaya stood in place of her imprisoned husband.

42149.q: Which president did Tsikhanouskaya stand against in 2020?
42149.e: Lukashenko has ruled Belarus since 1994 and had himself declared the winner in 2020 despite accusations of fraud.
42149.m: Lukashenko has ruled Belarus in an authoritarian way since 1994.

42150.q: Which neighbouring country did Tsikhanouskaya have to flee to after the 2020 election?
42150.e: Under pressure from the authorities she left Belarus and then lived in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania.
42150.m: Tsikhanouskaya had to go into exile in Lithuania in 2020.

42151.q: Which flag did many demonstrators in Belarus carry in 2020?
42151.e: The white-red-white flag was the flag of independent Belarus in the 1990s and became the symbol of the protests.
42151.m: The white-red-white flag became the sign of the Belarusian opposition.

42152.q: What did the European Parliament honour the opposition in Belarus for with a prize in 2020?
a: Its work for freedom and democracy
42152.e: The European Parliament awards the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought. In 2020 it went to the democratic opposition in Belarus.
42152.m: The Sakharov Prize honours people who fight for freedom.

42153.q: What happened to Tsikhanouskaya's husband Siarhei Tsikhanouski in June 2025?
a: He was sentenced to another 20 years
He founded a new party in Minsk
42153.e: After about five years in prison Siarhei Tsikhanouski was released in June 2025 and was able to leave for Lithuania.
42153.m: Siarhei Tsikhanouski was released in 2025 after years in prison.

42154.q: How many women together led the Belarusian opposition campaign in 2020?
42154.e: Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, Maria Kalesnikava and Veronika Tsepkalo appeared together after the male candidates had been put out of the race.
42154.m: Three women led the opposition in Belarus together in 2020.

42155.q: Which organisation holds the letter-writing marathon every year?
42155.e: In the letter-writing marathon people all over the world write letters for people whose human rights are being violated.
42155.m: Amnesty International organises the letter-writing marathon every year.

42156.q: Around which day of remembrance does the letter-writing marathon take place every year?
42156.e: On 10 December 1948 the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; the letter-writing marathon refers to this.
42156.m: The letter-writing marathon takes place around Human Rights Day.

42157.q: Who do participants in the letter-writing marathon mainly write to?
42157.e: The letters call on those responsible to release prisoners or end injustice; there are also letters of solidarity to the people affected.
42157.m: In the letter-writing marathon, letters call on the authorities to act.

42158.q: What does Amnesty International campaign for?
42158.e: Amnesty International fights worldwide against torture, the death penalty and unjust imprisonment. The letter-writing marathon is its best-known campaign.
42158.m: Amnesty International campaigns for human rights.

42159.q: How can young people take part in the letter-writing marathon?
42159.e: You can write letters to authorities or sign petitions. Many school classes take part every year.
42159.m: In the letter-writing marathon many letters help people in danger.

42160.q: What is Amnesty's letter-writing marathon called in English?
42160.e: Under the name “Write for Rights” people in many countries take part in the same campaign.
42160.m: The letter-writing marathon is called “Write for Rights” in English.

42161.q: What do the cases chosen for the letter-writing marathon stand for?
42161.e: Every year Amnesty presents specific people or groups whose rights are being violated, so that the letters have a face.
42161.m: The letter-writing marathon is about specific people whose rights are being violated.

42162.q: Which award did Amnesty International receive in 1977?
42162.e: In 1977 Amnesty was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for its work against torture and for political prisoners.
42162.m: Amnesty International received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977.

42163.q: What is a government in exile?
a: A government that works from abroad
A government made up only of foreigners
42163.e: A government in exile cannot work in its own country, for example because of occupation or dictatorship, so it works abroad.
42163.m: A government in exile works abroad because it cannot govern in its own country.

42164.q: In which city did several European governments in exile have their seat during the Second World War?
42164.e: The governments of Poland, Norway and the Netherlands, among others, fled to London from the German occupation.
42164.m: In the Second World War many governments in exile were based in London.

42165.q: In which country does the Tibetan government in exile have its seat?
42165.e: After the Dalai Lama fled in 1959, the Tibetan government in exile was set up in India. It is based in the town of Dharamsala.
42165.m: The Tibetan government in exile is based in India.

42166.q: The Dalai Lama fled from which country, which controls Tibet?
42166.e: China had occupied Tibet. After a failed uprising the Dalai Lama fled to India in 1959.
42166.m: The Dalai Lama fled from Chinese rule in Tibet.

42167.q: Which French general called from London in 1940 for resistance against the German occupation?
42167.e: On 18 June 1940 de Gaulle spoke on the BBC and then founded “Free France”.
42167.m: Charles de Gaulle led Free France from exile in London.

42168.q: Where did the Dutch queen flee to during the Second World War to escape the German occupation?
42168.e: Queen Wilhelmina fled to London in 1940. From there she spoke to her people on the radio.
42168.m: During the war the Dutch queen ruled from London.

42169.q: Why are governments in exile often supported by other states?
a: They are seen as the lawful representatives of their country
They provide soldiers for other countries
42169.e: Many states recognise a government in exile as the legitimate government when power in the country has been taken by occupation or force.
42169.m: Governments in exile see themselves as the lawful voice of their country.

42170.q: What did the King of Norway do when Germany occupied his country in 1940?
a: He went into exile in London with the government
He became a soldier in Germany
He gave his crown to the German emperor
42170.e: King Haakon VII refused to work with the occupiers. He led Norway from London and became a symbol of resistance.
42170.m: Norway's king resisted from exile in London.

42171.q: What is meant by civil disobedience?
a: Deliberately breaking a rule without violence for reasons of conscience
An armed uprising against the state
42171.e: In civil disobedience people break a rule publicly and without violence to draw attention to injustice.
42171.m: Civil disobedience deliberately breaks a rule without violence to expose injustice.

42172.q: What did the American Henry David Thoreau refuse to do in protest against slavery and war?
42172.e: Thoreau did not pay taxes because they helped to pay for slavery and war. He spent a night in prison for it and then wrote a famous essay on civil disobedience.
42172.m: Henry David Thoreau is seen as a pioneer of civil disobedience.

42173.q: Why was Rosa Parks arrested in Montgomery in 1955?
a: She would not give up her seat on the bus
She crossed the road at a red light
42173.e: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat to a white passenger; her arrest set off a bus boycott.
42173.m: Rosa Parks became famous for refusing to give up her seat on the bus.

42174.q: What followed the arrest of Rosa Parks in Montgomery in 1955?
42174.e: After the arrest, many black people in Montgomery, Alabama, stopped taking the bus for more than a year. After that, segregation on the buses was ended.
42174.m: The arrest of Rosa Parks was followed by the Montgomery bus boycott.

42175.q: Which civil rights campaigner wrote a famous letter from Birmingham jail in 1963?
42175.e: In the “Letter from Birmingham Jail” King defended breaking unjust laws without violence.
42175.m: Martin Luther King justified civil disobedience in a letter from prison.

42176.q: According to the classic view, what is part of civil disobedience?
a: You act only for your own benefit
42176.e: People who practise civil disobedience act openly and accept the legal consequences to show how serious their cause is.
42176.m: People who practise civil disobedience stand openly by their actions and the consequences.

42177.q: What did opponents of nuclear power occupy for several weeks in the canton of Aargau in 1975?
a: The building site of the planned Kaiseraugst nuclear power station
42177.e: Thousands of people occupied the building site without violence; the Kaiseraugst nuclear power station was in the end never built.
42177.m: The occupation of Kaiseraugst is a well-known example of civil disobedience in Switzerland.

42178.q: What do you call the protest in which people sit down and refuse to leave a place?
42178.e: In a sit-in protesters peacefully occupy a place; the 1960 sit-ins at lunch counters in Greensboro, USA, are well known.
42178.m: A sit-in is a peaceful sitting protest.

42179.q: How does civil disobedience differ from an authorised demonstration?
a: It always takes place at night
It is organised by the state
42179.e: An authorised demonstration is legal; civil disobedience deliberately crosses a rule but stays non-violent.
42179.m: Civil disobedience deliberately goes beyond permitted protest.

42180.q: What does a peaceful transfer of power mean in a democracy?
a: The losers of an election hand over the government without violence
The army decides the new government
The government stays in office for ever
42180.e: Whoever loses an election accepts the result and hands the office over to the winners in an orderly way.
42180.m: In a democracy power is handed on peacefully after elections.

42181.q: What did George Washington, the first President of the USA, do after two terms?
a: He gave up his office voluntarily
He handed the office to his son
42181.e: Washington declined a third term in 1797. In doing so he set an important example for the peaceful change of power.
42181.m: George Washington showed that power can be given up voluntarily.

42182.q: What does a new US president do before taking office?
a: He takes an oath of office
42182.e: With the oath of office the new president promises to protect the constitution. Traditionally this happens on 20 January.
42182.m: A new US president takes an oath at the start.

42183.q: What is a “round table” in politics?
a: Talks in which all sides negotiate as equals
A special piece of furniture in the Federal Palace
42183.e: At a round table there is no seat of honour, everyone is equal. In Poland in 1989 the government and opposition negotiated a peaceful change in this way.
42183.m: At a round table all sides negotiate as equals.

42184.q: What began the end of Augusto Pinochet's dictatorship in Chile in 1988?
42184.e: In a referendum the majority voted “No” to another term; in 1990 Pinochet handed power to an elected president.
42184.m: In Chile a vote ended the dictatorship peacefully.

42185.q: What happened in Spain after Franco's death in 1975?
42185.e: Without a civil war Spain became a democracy with free elections and a constitution from 1978. This period is called the Transición, meaning transition.
42185.m: After Franco, Spain peacefully became a democracy.

42186.q: Who ruled Chile from 1990, after the dictator Pinochet had given up power?
42186.e: Patricio Aylwin won the free election in 1989 and took over from Pinochet in March 1990.
42186.m: In 1990 Chile returned to democracy with a freely elected president.

42187.q: What did US President John Adams do when he lost the election to Thomas Jefferson in 1800?
a: He handed over the office peacefully
42187.e: Adams accepted his defeat and handed over the office in 1801. For the first time the governing party in the USA changed peacefully.
42187.m: In 1801 the governing party in the USA changed peacefully for the first time.

42188.q: In which country is there the powerful Guardian Council?
42188.e: The Guardian Council is a constitutional body of the Islamic Republic of Iran. It was created after the Islamic Revolution.
42188.m: The Guardian Council is an important body of power in Iran.

42189.q: Who sits on the Iranian Guardian Council?
42189.e: The Guardian Council has 12 members: 6 Islamic legal scholars and 6 other lawyers.
42189.m: Legal scholars and lawyers sit on the Guardian Council.

42190.q: Who appoints the six clerical members of the Guardian Council in Iran?
42190.e: The six Islamic legal scholars on the Guardian Council are appointed directly by the Supreme Leader, the “Leader of the Revolution”.
42190.m: The clerical members of the Guardian Council are chosen by the Supreme Leader.

42191.q: What does the Guardian Council check in every new law passed by the Iranian parliament?
a: Whether it is compatible with Islam
42191.e: The Guardian Council checks whether a law agrees with the rules of Islam and with the constitution. If not, it sends it back.
42191.m: The Guardian Council can stop laws it considers un-Islamic.

42192.q: What power does the Guardian Council have before elections in Iran?
a: It only prints the ballot papers
It has no task before elections
42192.e: Anyone in Iran who wants to stand for parliament or for president must be approved by the Guardian Council. Often many candidates are excluded.
42192.m: In Iran the Guardian Council decides who may stand for election at all.

42193.q: What are many senior clerics in Iran called?
42193.e: Ayatollah is an honorary title for senior Shia clerics. Iran's Supreme Leader also holds this title.
42193.m: Senior clerics in Iran are called Ayatollah.

42194.q: What do you call a state in which religious leaders hold the highest power, as in Iran?
42194.e: The word theocracy comes from Greek and means “rule by God”. In Iran clerics are at the head of the state.
42194.m: A theocracy is a state ruled by religious leaders.

42195.q: In which year was the Islamic Republic founded in Iran after a revolution?
42195.e: In 1979 the Shah was overthrown and Ayatollah Khomeini came to power. After that the Islamic Republic with the Guardian Council was created.
42195.m: The Islamic Republic of Iran has existed since 1979.

42196.q: The death of which young woman sparked huge protests in Iran in 2022?
42196.e: The young Kurdish woman died in police custody in Tehran in September 2022. Her death sparked protests across the country.
42196.m: The protests in Iran in 2022 began after the death of Jina Mahsa Amini.

42197.q: What did the protests in Iran in 2022 mainly stand for?
42197.e: After the death of 22-year-old Jina Mahsa Amini, many people protested against the strict dress rules and for more freedom.
42197.m: The protests in Iran in 2022 demanded freedom for women.

42198.q: Which police force had arrested Jina Mahsa Amini in 2022?
42198.e: In Iran the morality police enforced the strict dress rules. It accused Amini of breaking these rules.
42198.m: In Iran the morality police enforced the dress rules.

42199.q: Which slogan became famous during the protests in Iran in 2022?
42199.e: The slogan “Woman, Life, Freedom” originally comes from the Kurdish women's movement. It became a worldwide sign of the protests.
42199.m: “Woman, Life, Freedom” became the motto of the protests in Iran.

42200.q: Which rule for women was at the centre of the protests in Iran in 2022?
42200.e: In Iran women must wear a headscarf in public. During the protests many women took it off in public or burned it.
42200.m: The compulsory headscarf was a main reason for the protests in Iran.

42201.q: Which cry became the motto of the protests in Iran in 2022?
42201.e: “Woman, Life, Freedom” was chanted on the streets of Iran and all over the world. The cry stands for women's rights.
42201.m: The motto of the protests in Iran in 2022 was “Woman, Life, Freedom”.

42202.q: Which prize did the imprisoned Iranian women's rights activist Narges Mohammadi receive in 2023?
42202.e: Narges Mohammadi has campaigned for decades against the oppression of women in Iran. She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2023 while she was in prison.
42202.m: Narges Mohammadi received the Nobel Peace Prize in prison in 2023.

42203.q: How did the Iranian government react to the protests of 2022?
42203.e: Security forces cracked down violently on demonstrators. Thousands were arrested, and several protesters were even executed.
42203.m: Iran's leadership crushed the 2022 protests with violence.

42204.q: What did the Iranian government repeatedly block during the 2022 protests to make it harder for news to spread?
42204.e: The authorities blocked mobile internet and platforms such as Instagram and WhatsApp. This was to stop videos of the protests from getting abroad.
42204.m: Authoritarian governments often block the internet during protests.

42205.q: What form of government does Saudi Arabia have?
42205.e: In Saudi Arabia the king holds the highest power in government, law-making and the courts. There is no elected parliament.
42205.m: Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy.

42206.q: Which royal family is Saudi Arabia named after?
42206.e: The state was founded in 1932 by Abdulaziz ibn Saud. Since then the country has borne his family's name.
42206.m: Saudi Arabia bears the name of the Saud royal family.

42207.q: Who is King of Saudi Arabia (as of 2026)?
42207.e: King Salman has ruled Saudi Arabia since 2015. His son Mohammed bin Salman is crown prince and prime minister.
42207.m: Salman has been King of Saudi Arabia since 2015.

42208.q: What is the powerful Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman often called for short?
42208.e: Mohammed bin Salman is called MBS after his initials. He is regarded as the real ruler of the country.
42208.m: The Saudi crown prince is often called MBS.

42209.q: Since which year have women in Saudi Arabia been allowed to drive?
42209.e: For a long time Saudi Arabia was the only country where women were not allowed to drive. The ban was lifted in June 2018.
42209.m: Since 2018 women in Saudi Arabia have been allowed to drive.

42210.q: What role do political parties play in Saudi Arabia?
42210.e: There are no permitted political parties in Saudi Arabia. Power lies with the royal family.
42210.m: Political parties are not allowed in Saudi Arabia.

42211.q: What happened in 2018 to the Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, who had criticised the government?
a: He received a medal from the king
42211.e: Jamal Khashoggi was murdered in the Saudi consulate in Istanbul. The crime caused outrage around the world.
42211.m: The murder of Jamal Khashoggi showed how harshly Saudi Arabia deals with critics.

42212.q: What was the Saudi blogger Raif Badawi harshly punished for?
42212.e: Raif Badawi ran a liberal website. In 2014 he was sentenced to 10 years in prison and flogging, which sparked protests worldwide.
42212.m: Raif Badawi was harshly punished for his opinions on the internet.

42213.q: Who elects the parliament in Saudi Arabia?
a: Nobody, there is no elected parliament
The whole people every four years
42213.e: The Consultative Assembly, the Shura, is appointed by the king. It may give advice but cannot pass laws on its own.
42213.m: In Saudi Arabia there is no parliament elected by the people.

42214.q: What is Ashgabat, the capital of Turkmenistan, known for?
a: Lots of buildings made of white marble
42214.e: Ashgabat is the capital of Turkmenistan. The government had a great many splendid buildings made of white marble built there.
42214.m: Ashgabat is known for its white marble buildings.

42215.q: Turkmenistan's first president Niyazov called himself “Turkmenbashi”. What does that mean?
42215.e: Turkmenbashi means “Leader of the Turkmen”. Niyazov had himself worshipped like a ruler.
42215.m: Niyazov called himself “Leader of the Turkmen”.

42216.q: Among other things, what did Saparmurat Niyazov have renamed in Turkmenistan?
42216.e: Niyazov named months after himself and his mother. This is an example of an extreme personality cult.
42216.m: In Turkmenistan even months bore the ruler's name.

42217.q: Which book did schoolchildren in Turkmenistan have to learn under President Niyazov?
a: A book the president had written himself
A book of European fairy tales
42217.e: Niyazov wrote the book Ruhnama, the “Book of the Soul”. It was compulsory in schools and even in the driving test.
42217.m: In Turkmenistan children had to learn the president's book.

42218.q: Who succeeded Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov as President of Turkmenistan in 2022?
42218.e: In 2022 Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov handed the presidency to his son Serdar Berdimuhamedov. So power stayed in the family.
42218.m: In Turkmenistan power passed from father to son in 2022.

42219.q: Which raw material does Turkmenistan have in especially large amounts?
42219.e: Turkmenistan has some of the largest natural gas reserves in the world. The government uses the money to pay for splendid buildings.
42219.m: Turkmenistan is very rich in natural gas.

42220.q: What is the burning gas crater near Darvaza in Turkmenistan called?
42220.e: The crater in the Karakum Desert has been burning for decades because natural gas escapes there. It is a well-known sight.
42220.m: The Darvaza gas crater is called the “Gates of Hell”.

42221.q: Which desert covers a large part of Turkmenistan?
42221.e: The Karakum, “black sand”, covers most of the country.
42221.m: A large part of Turkmenistan is covered by the Karakum Desert.

42222.q: What did Russia's constitutional amendment of 2020 lay down about the relationship between Russian and international law?
a: The UN decides on Russian laws
42222.e: Since 2020, decisions by international bodies that contradict the Russian constitution no longer have to be carried out in Russia. This applies, for example, to rulings of international courts.
42222.m: Since 2020 Russia has put its constitution above decisions of international bodies.

42223.q: Thanks to the constitutional amendment of 2020, until what year could Vladimir Putin remain president?
42223.e: The amendment allowed Putin to stand again in the elections of 2024 and 2030. He was re-elected in 2024, and the second possible term would end in 2036.
42223.m: Putin could remain President of Russia until 2036.

42224.q: How long is one term of office for the Russian president?
42224.e: Since 2012 a term of office for the Russian president has lasted six years.
42224.m: The Russian president is elected for six years.

42225.q: What is the resetting of Putin's terms of office in the 2020 constitutional amendment often called?
42225.e: Putin's previous terms no longer count. That is why critics speak of the “zeroing” of his terms.
42225.m: With the zeroing, Putin's earlier terms no longer count.

42226.q: When did the vote on the constitutional amendment take place in Russia?
42226.e: The vote was postponed because of the coronavirus pandemic. It lasted a week and ended on 1 July 2020.
42226.m: Russians voted on the new constitution in summer 2020.

42227.q: What did independent observers criticise about the Russian constitutional vote of 2020?
a: That only women were allowed to vote
That the ballot papers were too colourful
42227.e: Officially about 78 per cent voted in favour. But independent observers reported many irregularities, such as people voting more than once.
42227.m: There were many irregularities in the 2020 vote in Russia.

42228.q: How has the Russian constitution defined marriage since 2020?
a: As a union of a man and a woman
As a union of any people
42228.e: The constitutional amendment laid down that marriage can only be between a man and a woman.
42228.m: Since 2020 the Russian constitution has defined marriage only as a union of a man and a woman.

42229.q: Which head of government resigned in January 2020 when Putin announced the constitutional amendment?
42229.e: Dmitry Medvedev resigned on the same day together with the whole government. Mikhail Mishustin became the new prime minister.
42229.m: Dmitry Medvedev resigned as Russian prime minister in 2020.

42230.q: Which country does Alexander Lukashenko rule?
42230.e: Alexander Lukashenko is President of Belarus.
42230.m: Alexander Lukashenko is the ruler of Belarus.

42231.q: How long has Alexander Lukashenko been ruling Belarus?
42231.e: Lukashenko won the presidential election in 1994. He has ruled the country without a break ever since.

42232.q: What is the capital of Belarus?
42232.e: Minsk is the capital and largest city of Belarus. The city lies roughly in the middle of the country.
42232.m: Minsk is the capital of Belarus.

42233.q: What happened to many of Lukashenko's critics after the 2020 election?
a: They were arrested or had to flee abroad
They were allowed to start their own newspaper
42233.e: After the protests thousands were arrested. Well-known opposition figures such as Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya fled into exile.
42233.m: In Belarus critics are arrested or driven into exile.

42234.q: What happened in Belarus after the presidential election in August 2020?
42234.e: Lukashenko declared himself the winner with about 80 per cent. Hundreds of thousands protested about election fraud, and many were arrested.
42234.m: In 2020 hundreds of thousands in Belarus protested against rigged elections.

42235.q: What did Belarus do in 2021 to arrest a journalist who criticised the regime?
a: It forced a passenger plane to land
It closed all its borders for a year
It offered him a ministerial post
42235.e: A Ryanair flight from Athens to Vilnius was forced to land in Minsk. There the journalist Roman Protasevich was arrested.
42235.m: In 2021 Belarus forced a passenger plane to land in order to arrest a critic.

42236.q: Which punishment does Belarus still have as the only country in Europe?
42236.e: Belarus is the only country in Europe that still executes people. That is one reason why it is not a member of the Council of Europe.
42236.m: Belarus is the only country in Europe that still carries out the death penalty.

42237.q: What other name was Belarus often known by in the past?
42237.e: In the past Belarus was often called Byelorussia, which means “White Russia”. The country lies between Poland and Russia.
42237.m: Belarus used to be called Byelorussia, or White Russia.

42238.q: What is the secret service in Belarus still called today, as in the days of the Soviet Union?
42238.e: Belarus has kept the name KGB for its secret service. It watches and persecutes opposition figures.
42238.m: In Belarus the secret service is still called the KGB.

42239.q: In which year did the Taliban take power in Afghanistan again?
42239.e: In August 2021 the Taliban captured the whole country while Western troops withdrew.
42239.m: The Taliban have ruled Afghanistan again since 2021.

42240.q: What is the capital of Afghanistan?
42240.e: Kabul is the capital and largest city of Afghanistan. The city lies in the east of the country at about 1,800 metres above sea level.
42240.m: Kabul is the capital of Afghanistan.

42241.q: What are girls in Afghanistan forbidden to do under the Taliban (as of 2026)?
42241.e: After year 6 girls are no longer allowed to go to school. Universities are also closed to women.
42241.m: Under the Taliban girls are not allowed to keep learning after primary school.

42242.q: When had the Taliban ruled Afghanistan before they returned in 2021?
42242.e: The Taliban first ruled from 1996 to 2001. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 they were overthrown by a US-led military operation.
42242.m: The first Taliban rule lasted from 1996 to 2001.

42243.q: Which famous cultural monuments did the Taliban destroy in 2001?
42243.e: The huge Buddha statues in Bamiyan were more than 1,400 years old. The Taliban blew them up because they reject images.
42243.m: The Taliban blew up the Buddhas of Bamiyan in 2001.

42244.q: What do the Taliban call their state in Afghanistan?
42244.e: The Taliban call their rule the “Islamic Emirate”. A religious leader is at its head.
42244.m: The Taliban call their state the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan.

42245.q: What must women in Afghanistan wear in public under the Taliban?
a: A covering for the face and body
42245.e: The Taliban require women to cover themselves completely in public, for example with a burka.
42245.m: The Taliban force women to cover themselves completely.

42246.q: Which Taliban ministry controls people's behaviour according to strict religious rules?
a: The Ministry of Virtue and Vice
42246.e: The Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice watches over clothing, beards and the behaviour of women.
42246.m: A Taliban morality authority watches over daily life.

42247.q: In which region of China do most Uyghurs live?
42247.e: Xinjiang is in north-west China. The Uyghurs are the largest ethnic group there.

42248.q: Which religion do most Uyghurs belong to?
42248.e: The Uyghurs are mostly Sunni Muslims. China heavily restricts the practice of their religion.

42249.q: Which language is the Uyghur language related to?
42249.e: Uyghur is a Turkic language. It is related to Turkish and Uzbek, not to Chinese.
42249.m: The Uyghurs speak a Turkic language.

42250.q: What does the Chinese government call the camps in which many Uyghurs are held?
42250.e: China officially calls the camps centres for vocational training. Human rights organisations speak of re-education camps.
42250.m: China officially calls the Uyghur camps training centres.

42251.q: According to estimates, how many Uyghurs and other Muslims were held in camps in Xinjiang?
42251.e: Researchers and human rights groups estimate that since 2017 about a million or more people have been in the camps.
42251.m: According to estimates, about a million Uyghurs were in camps.

42252.q: What conclusion did a 2022 report by the UN Human Rights Office reach about Xinjiang?
a: There might be crimes against humanity
42252.e: The report of August 2022 spoke of serious human rights violations that could be crimes against humanity. China rejected this.
42252.m: The UN sees possible crimes against humanity in Xinjiang.

42253.q: In which part of China is the region of Xinjiang, where the Uyghurs live?
42253.e: Xinjiang is in north-west China and borders countries such as Kazakhstan. The capital of the region is Ürümqi.

42254.q: Which farm product from Xinjiang is criticised because of accusations of forced labour?
42254.e: A large part of China's cotton comes from Xinjiang. There are accusations that Uyghurs are forced to work there.
42254.m: Cotton from Xinjiang is criticised because of forced labour.

42255.q: From which country was Hong Kong handed back to China in 1997?
42255.e: Hong Kong was a British colony for a long time. In 1997 it was handed back to the People's Republic of China.
42255.m: Hong Kong has belonged to China again since 1997.

42256.q: What was the principle that was meant to guarantee Hong Kong its own freedoms after 1997?
42256.e: China promised that Hong Kong would keep its own legal and economic system until 2047.
42256.m: “One country, two systems” was meant to protect Hong Kong's freedoms.

42257.q: Who passed the National Security Law for Hong Kong in 2020?
42257.e: The law was passed by the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress in Beijing, without Hong Kong's parliament.
42257.m: Hong Kong's National Security Law was passed in Beijing.

42258.q: What is the maximum sentence under Hong Kong's National Security Law of 2020?
42258.e: Serious cases of subversion, secession, terrorism or collusion with foreign forces can lead to life imprisonment.
42258.m: Under the National Security Law people in Hong Kong face life imprisonment.

42259.q: Which protests came before the National Security Law in Hong Kong?
42259.e: In 2019, according to the organisers, up to two million people demonstrated in Hong Kong, first against an extradition law and then for more democracy.
42259.m: The protests of 2019 were among the largest in Hong Kong's history.

42260.q: What happened in 2021 to the critical Hong Kong newspaper Apple Daily?
a: It won a court case against Beijing
42260.e: Apple Daily was critical of Beijing. After raids and the freezing of its accounts it had to close in June 2021.
42260.m: With Apple Daily, Hong Kong lost an important free newspaper in 2021.

42261.q: Which young activist became known as the face of the Hong Kong democracy movement?
42261.e: Joshua Wong became known at protests while he was still at school. In 2024 he was also sentenced to prison under the National Security Law.
42261.m: Joshua Wong became the face of the Hong Kong protests.

42262.q: What were the 2014 protests in Hong Kong called, named after an everyday object?
42262.e: The demonstrators protected themselves with umbrellas against police pepper spray. The umbrella became the symbol.
42262.m: In 2014 the umbrella became the symbol of the Hong Kong protests.

42263.q: What is the job of election observers?
a: To check whether an election is fair
42263.e: Election observers check independently whether elections are free, fair and follow the rules. Afterwards they write a report.
42263.m: Election observers check whether elections are fair.

42264.q: Which organisation, which Switzerland also belongs to, often sends election observers to Europe and Central Asia?
42264.e: The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) observes many elections in its member countries. Switzerland is a member.
42264.m: The OSCE observes elections in many countries.

42265.q: What do election observation teams publish after an election?
a: A report on how the election went
The names of all the voters
42265.e: The teams write down whether the election was free and fair and what problems there were. Many observation missions are organised by the OSCE's ODIHR in Warsaw.
42265.m: Election observers describe in a report whether an election was fair.

42266.q: What do election observers watch for in polling stations on election day, for example?
a: Whether votes are cast secretly and correctly
Whether voters have breakfast on time
Whether the ballot papers are colourful
42266.e: It is important that every person can vote in secret and that the votes are counted correctly.
42266.m: In a fair election people vote in secret and the votes are counted correctly.

42267.q: What is a sign of election fraud that observers would report?
a: One person puts several ballot papers in the box
The polling station opens on time
The polling staff wear name badges
42267.e: When someone puts several papers in the ballot box, it is called ballot stuffing. It distorts the result.
42267.m: Several ballot papers from one person are election fraud.

42268.q: Why do some authoritarian states not invite independent election observers?
a: So that irregularities are not noticed
Because they have too few hotels
Because observers only work in summer
42268.e: Without independent observers it is easier to hide fraud. The government can then claim a good result.
42268.m: A state that allows no election observers makes itself look suspicious.

42269.q: What do you call observers who are in the country weeks before an election?
42269.e: Long-term observers follow the election campaign, the media and the preparations. Short-term observers only come for election day.
42269.m: Long-term observers follow an election long before election day.

42270.q: What do you call an election whose result is fixed in advance because there is no real choice?
42270.e: In a sham election people only pretend that the population can decide. Election observers criticise such elections.
42270.m: A sham election is not a real election.

42271.q: What does it mean when a ruler's assets are “frozen”?
a: He can no longer use his money
His money is put in a fridge
42271.e: When an account is frozen, the person may no longer access their money or property. But it is not taken away.
42271.m: Frozen assets stay blocked but still belong to the owner.

42272.q: Who decides in Switzerland whether the country adopts sanctions against a ruler?
42272.e: The Federal Council decides which sanctions Switzerland adopts. They are carried out by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO).
42272.m: In Switzerland the Federal Council decides on sanctions.

42273.q: Whose sanctions does Switzerland often join, even though it is not a member?
42273.e: Switzerland is not in the EU but often adopts its sanctions, for example against Russia from February 2022.
42273.m: Switzerland often adopts the EU's sanctions.

42275.q: Which UN body can impose sanctions that are binding on all member countries?
42275.e: The UN Security Council can impose sanctions that all members must follow. Each of the five permanent members can block this with a veto.
42275.m: The UN Security Council can impose binding sanctions.

42276.q: What is an entry ban as a sanction?
a: The person may not enter a country
The person may not leave their house
The person may no longer make phone calls
The person may no longer eat
